title: Direct vs Regular Mutual Funds: Understanding SEBI's Default Rule
description: Regular mutual funds include distributor commissions, leading to higher annual expense ratios. Direct mutual funds allow you to invest directly with the Asset.

faq.q: What is the primary difference between direct and regular mutual funds?
faq.a: The main difference lies in the expense ratio. Regular plans include distributor commissions, making their expense ratios higher, while direct plans have lower expense ratios as you invest directly with the AMC without an intermediary.

faq.q: How does SEBI's new default plan rule work?
faq.a: From November 1, 2026, when you invest in mutual funds through an AMC's digital platform, the 'Direct Plan' will be the default selection. If you don't explicitly choose a plan, your investment will be processed as a Direct Plan.

faq.q: Will my existing regular mutual fund investments automatically convert to direct plans?
faq.a: No, SEBI's new rule applies to new investments made via AMC digital platforms. Your existing Regular Plan investments or ongoing SIPs will not automatically convert to Direct Plans.

faq.q: Are direct plans always better than regular plans?
faq.a: From a cost perspective, direct plans are always more cost-efficient due to lower expense ratios, which can lead to higher returns over time. However, regular plans offer the service and advice of a distributor, which can be valuable for investors who prefer professional guidance.

faq.q: What should I consider before switching my existing regular plan units to direct plans?
faq.a: Before switching, consider the capital gains tax implications (Short-Term Capital Gains or Long-Term Capital Gains, depending on holding period and fund type) and any applicable exit loads. A switch is treated as a redemption and re-investment.

faq.q: Where can I invest in direct mutual funds?
faq.a: You can invest in direct mutual funds directly through the websites or mobile applications of individual Asset Management Companies (AMCs), through platforms like MFUtility (MFU), or via Registered Investment Advisers (RIAs) who operate on a fee-only model.
